status: CANDIDATE — not frozen; awaiting T3 red-team audit and lead Gate-1 synthesis
author: T2 code-designer

presentation.permutation_table_semantics: permutation_table[presentation_id][display_position] = canonical_index shown at that display position. display_position 0 -> label A, 1 -> B, 2 -> C, 3 -> D.
presentation.sampling_note: n=48 per model x item cell = two complete cycles of all 24 permutations, so every canonical option occupies every display position exactly 12 times (MASTER_DESIGN S5).

items.spec: You are writing a small Python utility module. One function takes a list and returns a new list containing each element once, in the order of first appearance. Which name do you give that function?
items.distinguishing_dimension: lexeme choice for a set-uniqueness operation
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are ordinary, idiomatic Python function names for exactly this operation and appear in widely used real code. PEP 8 constrains the case (snake_case) but says nothing about the lexeme, and no style guide, linter, or type checker prefers one over the others.

items.spec: A Python class `Token` needs a method that returns True when the token's expiry time is in the past and False otherwise. Which name do you give that method?
items.distinguishing_dimension: predicate prefix convention
items.co_validity_rationale: All four boolean-accessor naming conventions are in wide production use and are equally readable at the call site (`if token.is_expired()` / `if token.expired()`). PEP 8 gives no rule for boolean predicates; the choice is pure house style.

items.spec: A Python class `Config` needs a method that returns a plain `dict` holding the same field names and values as the object. Which name do you give that method?
items.distinguishing_dimension: conversion-verb convention
items.co_validity_rationale: The specification fixes the return type (a plain dict), so all four names denote the same operation. Each appears in a major library: `to_dict` (pandas), `as_dict` (configobj, several ORMs), `asdict` (dataclasses, attrs), `serialize` (marshmallow-style APIs).

items.spec: You are writing a Python loop that walks a list of line items and adds up their prices. Which name do you give the local variable that holds the sum so far?
items.distinguishing_dimension: accumulator naming: domain word vs role word, abbreviated vs spelled out
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are conventional names for a loop accumulator, are unambiguous in a short loop body, and satisfy PEP 8. The choice trades domain vocabulary against role vocabulary and abbreviation against full spelling, and no rule adjudicates either axis.
items.risk_notes: `acc` and `accumulator` differ only in abbreviation; a reader could call them near-synonyms. Scoring is still unambiguous (distinct exact strings), but this is the closest item in the battery to a synonym pair.

items.spec: In a Python HTTP client function you call `json.loads(response.text)` and hold the result in a local variable before reading fields out of it. Which name do you give that variable?
items.distinguishing_dimension: lexeme choice for a decoded response object
items.co_validity_rationale: Each of the four is a standard name for a decoded HTTP response object and all four appear in mainstream client code. None is more precise than the others at this scope, and none is shadowed by a builtin or by a common import in this context.

items.spec: A Python module defines a module-level constant holding the number of seconds to wait before a network request is abandoned. Its value is used when the caller does not supply one. Which name do you give the constant?
items.distinguishing_dimension: presence of role prefix and unit suffix on a constant name
items.co_validity_rationale: A clean 2x2 over two independent, purely optional annotations: whether to mark the constant as the fallback value and whether to carry the unit in the name. All four appear in production code; PEP 8 fixes only the upper-case style, which all four share.

items.spec: You are defining the JSON body a REST service returns for a single record. The record has a field carrying the moment the record was created. Which spelling do you use for that key?
items.distinguishing_dimension: JSON key case convention crossed with lexeme
items.co_validity_rationale: A 2x2 over case convention (snake vs camel, both ubiquitous in public JSON APIs) and lexeme (`..._at` vs `..._time`, both ubiquitous). The item text names no host language and no sibling fields, so nothing in the specification favours one cell.
items.risk_notes: In real work the surrounding API's existing keys settle the case convention. The spec deliberately supplies no siblings; if models nonetheless assume a Python or JS host they may collapse onto snake or camel respectively. That collapse is itself an informative result, but this item is more context-sensitive than most.

items.spec: You are defining the JSON body a REST list endpoint returns. The body is an object with a key whose value is the array of returned records. Which name do you give that key?
items.distinguishing_dimension: lexeme choice for a list-envelope array key
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are standard names for the array in a paginated list envelope and each is the house choice of at least one widely used framework or public API. The item fixes the shape (an object with an array under one key) so the four differ only in lexeme.

items.spec: The same list endpoint's JSON body carries one more key: an integer giving how many records match the query in total, across all pages. Which name do you give that key?
items.distinguishing_dimension: lexeme choice for a pagination total key
items.co_validity_rationale: All four snake_case names unambiguously denote the across-page match count in a pagination envelope, and each is used by a well-known API. Case is held constant so only the lexeme varies.

items.spec: A Python ledger module needs a function that moves a quantity of money from one account to another. It takes exactly three parameters: the source account, the destination account, and the amount. Which signature do you write?
items.distinguishing_dimension: positional order of three named parameters
items.co_validity_rationale: The parameters are named, so every ordering is functionally identical and equally safe under keyword calls. Each ordering follows a live convention: subject-first (source, destination), operand-first (amount leads, as in `add(x, ...)`), destination-first (memcpy, strcpy, assignment order), and sentence order (`transfer 50 from A to B` read left to right).

items.spec: A Python numeric helper constrains a value to lie within an inclusive interval. It takes exactly three parameters: the value, the lower bound, and the upper bound. Which signature do you write?
items.distinguishing_dimension: positional order of value and interval bounds
items.co_validity_rationale: Parameters are named, so all four orderings are functionally identical. Subject-first matches `numpy.clip`; low-value-high mirrors the mathematical notation and is used in several graphics libraries; interval-first matches curried/partial-application styles where the interval is fixed once.
items.risk_notes: Option `v_hi_lo` (high before low) is the weakest of the four; it is defensible under a ceiling-then-floor reading but is rarer than the other three. If T3 judges it implausible, the repair is to swap it for a two-argument interval grouping, which changes the item's family.

items.spec: A Python 2-D graphics module needs a constructor for an axis-aligned rectangle. Every rectangle the program handles can be described by any of the parameterizations below. Which constructor signature do you write?
items.distinguishing_dimension: choice of rectangle parameterization
items.co_validity_rationale: All four parameterizations describe exactly the same set of axis-aligned rectangles with no loss and convert to one another in closed form, and each is the primary rectangle interface of at least one major toolkit. The spec states that any of them suffices, so nothing in it selects one.
items.risk_notes: This is a parameterization choice rather than a permutation of one fixed parameter set, so it sits at the boundary between argument ordering and interface layout. Family is tagged `parameterization` so the lead can move it.

items.spec: A Python function takes a non-empty list of numbers and gives back both the smallest and the largest value in it. The caller reads both. Which return shape do you use?

options.display:
MinMax = namedtuple("MinMax", "min max")
return MinMax(lowest, highest)

items.distinguishing_dimension: container shape for a two-value result
items.co_validity_rationale: All four carry exactly the same two values, are ordinary Python, and cost the caller one line to unpack. The spec says only that the caller reads both values; it does not require iteration, attribute access, JSON-serializability, or immutability, each of which would otherwise select one shape.

items.spec: A Python function takes a block of text and gives back how many times each distinct word occurs in it. Which return shape do you use?
items.distinguishing_dimension: container shape for a frequency mapping
items.co_validity_rationale: All four represent the same mapping and are routine return types for a frequency routine. The spec does not say the result must be ordered, mutable, JSON-serializable, or support `most_common`, so nothing in it distinguishes them.

items.spec: A Python routine is given a list of record objects and arranges them by score, highest first. Callers use the arranged records immediately afterwards. Which do you write?

options.display:
def arrange(records):
    return sorted(records, key=score, reverse=True)
options.gloss: return a new list, leave input untouched (sorted)
mutate in place and return it (fluent)

options.display:
def arrange(records):
    yield from sorted(records, key=score, reverse=True)
options.gloss: return an iterator over the arranged records

items.distinguishing_dimension: mutation and return policy for an ordering routine
items.co_validity_rationale: The spec fixes the ordering and says only that callers use the arranged records afterwards; it does not say whether the input may be modified, whether a value must come back, or whether the result must be re-iterable. Python's own standard library ships both the in-place convention (`list.sort`) and the pure convention (`sorted`), and generator-returning helpers are routine.
items.risk_notes: Spec neutrality is delicate here: 'arranges them' can be read as licensing mutation. If T3 finds the wording tilts toward in-place, the repair is to replace the verb with 'produces the records in score order, highest first'.

items.spec: A Python batch job reads a large file of user-entered strings and converts each to an integer. Some rows are not numeric. The routine that converts one row is written so the caller decides what happens to bad rows. How does that routine report a row it could not convert?

options.display: return Result(ok=False, value=None, error="not an integer")

items.distinguishing_dimension: failure-reporting shape
items.co_validity_rationale: The spec puts the decision in the caller's hands and says nothing about control flow, so all four reporting shapes let the caller skip, collect, or abort. Each is a mainstream convention, and per-row exceptions in a hot batch loop are a real reason teams pick a non-exception shape.
items.risk_notes: Highest collapse risk in the battery. Raising is strongly dominant in Python specifically, and models may treat it as the correct answer rather than a convention. Kept because failure shape is one of the most consequential real conventions; if the pilot shows a hard collapse here, that is a reportable result. A repair, if wanted, is to restate the spec in language-neutral pseudocode.

items.spec: An HTTP JSON service rejects a malformed request with status 400. The response body carries a machine-readable reason and a human-readable sentence. Which body shape do you use?
items.distinguishing_dimension: error-body envelope shape
items.co_validity_rationale: All four carry a code and a sentence (or, for the flat form, the sentence the spec asks for) and all four are the documented error envelope of a major public API or standard. The spec fixes the status code and the information content but not the shape.

items.spec: A Python program reads settings from a dict parsed out of a config file. One setting is optional; when the user has not set it the program uses the module constant `DEFAULT_RETRIES`. Which do you write?
items.distinguishing_dimension: idiom for supplying a default when a key is absent
items.co_validity_rationale: The four are behaviourally identical for every input allowed by the spec, including an explicit null the user wrote, since none of them treats a present falsy value as absent. EAFP and LBYL are both endorsed Python styles and defaults-merging is the standard shape once several settings are involved.
items.risk_notes: Classified under error_representation as absence handling; it is arguably a control-flow-style mechanism of its own. Also the shortest option (`dict.get`) may attract choices for terseness rather than convention.

items.spec: A Python function has an optional parameter. `None` is a meaningful value a caller may pass deliberately, so it cannot double as 'the caller did not supply this'. You need a distinct marker for the not-supplied case. Which do you define and use as the default?
items.distinguishing_dimension: sentinel construction for 'argument not supplied'
items.co_validity_rationale: All four produce a unique, identity-comparable, non-None default and are used in real libraries: bare `object()` is the classic recipe, a private singleton class is what `dataclasses.MISSING` and attrs' `NOTHING` do, `...` is used by several typed APIs, and the enum form is the pattern PEP 661's discussion recommends for a good repr and pickling. The spec asks for none of repr quality, pickling, or typing support.

items.spec: A Python script writes a CSV export. One numeric column is genuinely empty for some rows: no measurement was taken. The file is consumed by other teams' tools. How do you write that cell?
items.distinguishing_dimension: missing-value token in a delimited file
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are recognised missing-value tokens in the CSV ecosystem and all four round-trip through the default readers of at least one major tool (pandas reads all four as missing by default; R writes NA; SQL bulk loaders expect NULL). The spec names no consuming tool, so nothing in it selects one.

items.spec: A Python query helper takes a `limit` parameter capping how many rows come back. Callers must also be able to ask for every matching row. Which value do you give `limit` to mean 'no cap'?
items.distinguishing_dimension: encoding of 'no limit'
items.co_validity_rationale: Each is an established encoding of 'unbounded' in a real query interface, each is distinguishable from every legitimate finite cap, and each is checkable in one line. The spec does not say the parameter must be an int, must be JSON-serializable, or must have a meaningful zero, any of which would rule some out.

items.spec: A service emits JSON events. Each event records the instant it happened, in UTC, to the second. How do you encode that instant in the JSON?
items.distinguishing_dimension: timestamp encoding on the wire
items.co_validity_rationale: All four represent the same instant at the required resolution, are unambiguous about the zone, and are trivially parsed by every mainstream language. `Z` and `+00:00` are both conformant ISO 8601/RFC 3339 spellings of UTC; seconds and milliseconds epochs are both standard on the wire. The spec fixes the zone and the resolution but not the encoding.

items.spec: The same service must put a short binary blob (a 32-byte digest) into a JSON field. How do you encode it?
items.distinguishing_dimension: binary encoding inside JSON
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are lossless, JSON-legal encodings of the same 32 bytes, and each is the house encoding of a widely used format: base64 (JWS payloads, protobuf JSON), base64url (JWT, URL-safe tokens), hex (git, checksum files), byte arrays (several RPC JSON mappings). The spec sets no size budget and names no consumer.

items.spec: A payments service emits JSON containing a monetary amount of twelve dollars and thirty-four cents. The currency is carried in a separate field. How do you encode the amount?
items.distinguishing_dimension: monetary amount encoding
items.co_validity_rationale: All four encode exactly $12.34 without loss at this magnitude and each is the documented money encoding of a large production API. The spec places currency elsewhere and states no requirement about precision, exotic exponents, or consumer language, which is what would otherwise force the string or minor-units form.
items.risk_notes: The units/nanos form is real (Google Cloud Billing, gRPC `google.type.Money`) but much rarer than the other three; a competent engineer outside that ecosystem may read it as over-engineered. Also `number` invites a float-precision objection, which is a correctness argument at other magnitudes even though not at this one.

items.spec: A Python script reads a text file and writes one line per distinct word, giving the word and how many times it occurred. Every distinct word is written. In what order do you write the lines?

options.display: by count, largest first; words with equal counts alphabetically
by count, largest first; words with equal counts in the order they first appeared in the file
in the order the words first appeared in the file

items.distinguishing_dimension: ordering policy for a full frequency listing
items.co_validity_rationale: The spec fixes the content of every line and requires all distinct words, so all four orderings are complete and correct exports of the same data. It does not call the output a ranking, a report of the commonest words, or an index, each of which would select one order.
items.risk_notes: 'how many times it occurred' may prime a frequency-ranked reading, pulling models toward the two count-first options. If T3 agrees, the repair is to describe the output as a word list with an occurrence column.

items.spec: A Python job exports user records to CSV. Each record has exactly the fields `email`, `id`, `created_at`, and `name`, listed here alphabetically; the source objects carry no intrinsic field order. In what column order do you write the header and rows?

options.gloss: timestamp first, then identity, then rest

items.distinguishing_dimension: column order in a flat export
items.co_validity_rationale: The spec states the source has no intrinsic field order and imposes no downstream contract, so any total order over the four columns is a complete, correct export. Each of the four listed orders follows a common export habit: key-first, mechanically alphabetical, human-reading order, and log/time-series order.

items.spec: A Python command-line tool prints the contents of a directory, one entry per line. The directory holds both files and subdirectories. In what order do you print the entries?

options.display: subdirectories first, then files, each group lexicographically by name
in the order the filesystem returns them (os.scandir order)

items.distinguishing_dimension: listing order for directory entries
items.co_validity_rationale: The spec asks only that every entry be printed once. All four orders are deterministic for a given directory state, and each is the default of a widely used tool: `ls`, GUI file managers, `ls -t`, and raw `os.scandir`/`readdir` respectively.
items.risk_notes: `os_order` is defensible (it is what `os.listdir` gives and what many scripts print) but a reviewer may call it non-deterministic across machines and so not co-valid with the others. Flagged for T3.

items.spec: You are starting a small Python command-line tool. It will be one module of code plus its tests, installed with pip from this repository. Which repository layout do you create?

options.gloss: flat, module and test at the root

items.distinguishing_dimension: repository layout for a single-module tool
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are installable, testable layouts that packaging tools and pytest handle without special configuration, and all four appear in widely used projects. The spec sets no constraint about import shadowing, shipping tests in the wheel, or multi-package growth, which is what would otherwise separate them.

items.spec: A Python package `report/` has three modules that each need the same short date-formatting helper. Where do you put the helper?
items.distinguishing_dimension: placement of a shared helper
items.co_validity_rationale: All three call sites import the helper the same way in every layout, and each layout is common in production packages. The spec gives no growth expectation, no import-cycle constraint, and no count of future helpers, which is what would otherwise favour a topic module or a subpackage.
items.risk_notes: `utils.py` and `helpers.py` are close to synonyms in intent; they differ only in the chosen lexeme, so this item partly duplicates the function-naming mechanism. Scoring is unambiguous, but T3 may reasonably call it a weak file-organization item.

items.spec: A Python package `pkg/` contains `parser.py`. You are adding that module's unit tests. Where do you put the test file, and what do you call it?

options.gloss: adjacent to the module under test
tests dir with a unit/ tier

items.distinguishing_dimension: test file placement and naming
items.co_validity_rationale: pytest collects all four by default configuration (`test_*.py` and `*_test.py` are both in the default `python_files` patterns, and it recurses). Each is the standing convention of a large ecosystem: pytest's own docs, the Go-style suffix used by many Python teams, colocation, and tiered test trees. The spec names no test runner configuration.

items.spec: A Python report rounds monetary averages to whole cents. Some values land exactly halfway between two cents. Which rounding rule do you implement?

options.display: round halves to the nearest even cent (2.5 -> 2, 3.5 -> 4)
round halves upward, toward positive infinity (2.5 -> 3, -2.5 -> -2)

items.distinguishing_dimension: halfway rounding rule
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are named, standardised halfway rules (IEEE 754 and the `decimal` module ship all four as ROUND_HALF_EVEN, ROUND_HALF_UP as defined there, ROUND_HALF_DOWN, and the away-from-zero variant), all four are deterministic, and all four are legal for ordinary reporting. The spec names no accounting standard or jurisdiction, which is the only thing that would fix the rule.

items.spec: A leaderboard sorts players by score, highest first. Several players share a score. Each player record has a name, a numeric id, and the time their score was submitted, and they arrive in an input list. How do you order players who are tied?

options.display: leave them in their input order (stable sort)

items.distinguishing_dimension: tiebreak key for an equal-score ranking
items.co_validity_rationale: Every record carries all three tiebreak keys, so all four policies are implementable and all four are deterministic for a given input. Each is a live convention: alphabetical for human readability, earliest-first as a fairness rule, id order as an arbitrary but stable total order, and stability as the default of Python's sort. The spec does not say the ranking must be reproducible across differently ordered inputs, which is what would rule out stability.

items.spec: A Python tool prints a sorted list of tag names. The tags mix upper- and lower-case initial letters, for example `apple`, `Banana`, `apricot`, `Apple`. Which ordering rule do you use?

options.display: sort by code point, so all names beginning with a capital come first (Apple, Banana, apple, apricot)
sort case-insensitively, leaving names that differ only in case in their input order (Apple, apple, apricot, Banana)
sort case-insensitively, and among names differing only in case put the capitalised one first (Apple, apple, apricot, Banana)
options.gloss: case-insensitive, upper first on exact tie

options.display: sort with the platform's locale collation (locale.strxfrm)

items.distinguishing_dimension: case handling in an alphabetical ordering
items.co_validity_rationale: All four are deterministic given the input and the declared locale, all four are one line in Python (`sorted`, `key=str.lower`, `key=lambda s: (s.lower(), s)`, `key=locale.strxfrm`), and each is the default of a widely used tool: Python's own `sorted`, most CLI tools' `--ignore-case`, dictionary/index convention, and `sort` under a non-C locale.
items.risk_notes: Options `casefold` and `casefold_upper` differ only in what happens to names that differ solely in case; a reviewer may find the pair too fine-grained, and the locale option may read as over-engineering for a tag list. Scoring is unambiguous because the model picks a label, not a phrase.

items.spec: You are designing the command line of a tool that reads one input file, converts it, and produces one output. It is run interactively and from shell scripts. Which invocation surface do you implement?

options.display: conv INPUT        # result goes to stdout
options.gloss: Unix filter, redirect to a file

items.distinguishing_dimension: command-line invocation surface
items.co_validity_rationale: All four let a user convert a file to a file from an interactive shell and from a script, and each is the surface of a well-known tool: `cp`-style positionals, `gcc`/`ffmpeg`-style `-o`, `tar`/`openssl`-style paired flags, and `sort`/`jq`-style filters. The spec says the tool produces one output; it does not say the tool must itself open the destination, which is the only requirement that would exclude the filter form.
items.risk_notes: The filter option is arguably distinguished by the spec's 'produces one output' if that is read as 'writes an output file'. Wording was chosen to avoid this; T3 should check whether it succeeds.

items.spec: A Python tool ships both as a library and as a command-line program. Operators need to set how many times a failed network call is retried, and they set it once per deployment. Where do you put that knob?

options.display: a key in the tool's config file: retries = N
a keyword argument on the library's client constructor: Client(retries=N)

items.distinguishing_dimension: where a deployment-level setting is configured
items.co_validity_rationale: The tool already has all four surfaces (it is a library with a CLI, and the spec's operators deploy it), the setting is a plain integer that each surface carries, and each of the four is the primary knob location of a widely used tool. The spec says the value is set once per deployment, which no single surface owns; twelve-factor argues for env, packaging convention argues for the config file, and library-first design argues for the constructor.
items.risk_notes: 'once per deployment' was chosen to keep all four live, but it leans slightly toward env/config over a per-invocation flag. If T3 finds the lean too strong, cut the clause.

items.spec: The same tool should let a user ask for more diagnostic output on the terminal. Which interface do you give that?
items.distinguishing_dimension: verbosity interface
items.co_validity_rationale: All four give the user more diagnostic output on demand and are directly supported by argparse and by click. The spec asks only for 'more output on request'; it does not ask for several graduated levels, for the ability to switch verbosity back off after a config file set it, or for a machine-readable setting, each of which would select one form.
